name: Hiroki Haraguchi
bio: Proposed metallomics as an integrated field for studying metals and metal-containing biomolecules. His foundational 2004 paper connects elemental analysis and chemical speciation with the questions raised by genomics and proteomics.
affiliation: Nagoya University · Nagoya, Japan

name: Robert J. P. Williams
bio: Helped establish bioinorganic chemistry and the Irving–Williams stability series. His work connected metal coordination, enzyme function and biological evolution, providing a chemical foundation for understanding why cells use particular elements.
affiliation: University of Oxford · Oxford, UK

name: Barry P. Rosen
bio: Studies how organisms transport, transform and detoxify arsenic and other metals. His work on arsenic uptake, efflux, biomethylation and organoarsenical chemistry links bacterial resistance mechanisms to environmental exposure. FIU records his retirement in 2025.
affiliation: Florida International University · Miami, USA

name: Marc Solioz
bio: Investigated the copper-handling cop operon in Enterococcus hirae, including the CopY repressor, CopZ chaperone and CopA/CopB ATPases. This work helped connect copper transport, intracellular delivery and gene regulation. The linked publication documents his research at Bern.
affiliation: University of Bern · Bern, Switzerland

name: Nigel J. Robinson
bio: Leading theorist of protein "metalation" — how cells ensure each metalloprotein gets the correct metal — and of metal-sensing regulators such as the nickel sensor InrS.
affiliation: Durham University · Durham, UK

name: David P. Giedroc
bio: Investigates how bacteria sense and manage metals, reactive sulfur species and oxidative stress. His laboratory combines structural biology, spectroscopy and biochemistry to explain the regulatory switches that keep essential metal chemistry under control.
affiliation: Indiana University Bloomington · Bloomington, USA

name: Amy C. Rosenzweig
role: Professor of Molecular Biosciences and Chemistry
bio: Investigates metalloprotein function with structural, spectroscopic, biochemical and genetic methods. Major interests include biological methane oxidation, oxygen activation, metal uptake and transport, and the biosynthesis of metal-binding natural products.
affiliation: Northwestern University · Evanston, USA

name: Valeria C. Culotta
bio: Investigates how metals and reactive oxygen species shape the interaction between hosts and fungal pathogens. Her laboratory studies copper, manganese, iron and superoxide dismutases, with particular attention to Candida albicans and Candida auris.
affiliation: Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health · Baltimore, USA

name: Thomas V. O'Halloran
bio: Investigates the cell biology and coordination chemistry of metals, including intracellular metal trafficking, zinc dynamics and copper homeostasis. His work on metallochaperones helped explain how cells deliver reactive metal ions to the proteins that need them.
affiliation: Michigan State University · East Lansing, USA

name: Deborah B. Zamble
bio: Investigated how bacteria acquire and deliver nickel to enzymes, including the metallochaperones involved in hydrogenase maturation. Her work helped explain the coordination between metal sensing, transport and enzyme assembly. This historical entry commemorates her contributions.
affiliation: University of Toronto · Toronto, Canada

name: Kevin J. Waldron
role: Professor of IBB PAS; Head of Laboratory
bio: Studies how metalloproteins acquire the correct metal and how metal specificity evolves. Current laboratory work includes superoxide dismutases, bacterial metal homeostasis and the consequences of metal starvation for enzyme function.
affiliation: Polish Academy of Sciences (IBB) · Warsaw, Poland

name: Amit R. Reddi
bio: Investigates the cellular mechanisms that activate metalloproteins and regulate their signaling functions. His laboratory focuses on heme trafficking and copper/zinc superoxide dismutase, using chemical biology to connect metal availability with metabolism and disease.
affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology · Atlanta, USA

name: Christopher Rensing
bio: Studies metal–microbe interactions across environmental and medical settings. His research connects bacterial metal resistance with electromicrobiology and bioremediation. ASM identifies him as a distinguished professor and director of the Institute of Environmental Microbiology at FAFU.
affiliation: Fujian Agriculture & Forestry University · Fuzhou, China

name: Dietrich H. Nies
bio: Investigates how bacteria maintain metal balance in highly contaminated environments. Work with Cupriavidus metallidurans and its metal-efflux systems has helped explain how microbes tolerate metals and transform their surrounding chemistry.
affiliation: Martin-Luther-University Halle-Wittenberg · Halle, Germany

name: John D. Helmann
bio: Uses Bacillus subtilis to study cellular responses to metal deficiency, metal excess, reactive oxygen species and antibiotics. His laboratory examines transcriptional regulation and the molecular sensors that coordinate these stress responses.
affiliation: Cornell University · Ithaca, USA

name: Katherine J. Franz
role: James B. Duke Distinguished Professor of Chemistry
bio: Investigates how biological systems manage the coordination chemistry of essential but potentially toxic metals, especially copper and iron. Her laboratory develops chemical tools to change metal location, speciation and reactivity, including approaches relevant to microbial pathogens.
affiliation: Duke University · Durham, USA

name: Lucia Banci
bio: Uses structural biology and NMR to study metal ions, protein maturation and intracellular metal trafficking. Her group developed in-cell NMR approaches that allow proteins to be examined in living cells at atomic resolution.
affiliation: University of Florence · Florence, Italy

name: Caryn E. Outten
role: Professor; Guy F. Lipscomb Professor of Chemistry
bio: Studies how cells sense and distribute iron, with an emphasis on iron–sulfur clusters and glutaredoxin proteins. Her research connects the chemistry of these cofactors with iron regulation, redox balance and cellular stress.
affiliation: University of South Carolina · Columbia, USA

name: James A. Imlay
bio: Studies how reactive oxygen species damage bacteria and how cells defend themselves. His work connects oxidative stress with iron-containing enzymes, metal availability and the repair or protection of vulnerable metabolic pathways.
affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign · Urbana, USA

name: Lena J. Daumann
role: W3 Professor & Chair of Bioinorganic Chemistry
bio: A leader in lanthanide microbiology; characterized how methylotrophic and methanotrophic bacteria use rare-earth elements as catalytic cofactors in methanol dehydrogenase.
affiliation: Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf · Düsseldorf, Germany

name: Joseph A. Cotruvo Jr.
bio: Studies how bacteria recognize, acquire and use rare-earth elements. Research on the lanthanide-binding protein lanmodulin links microbial metal selectivity with protein engineering and opportunities for biological rare-earth separation.
affiliation: Pennsylvania State University · University Park, USA

name: Stéphane L. Benoit
bio: Investigates nickel acquisition, storage and nickel-dependent enzymes in bacterial pathogens. His work on Helicobacter and Campylobacter connects hydrogenase and urease biology with host colonization, respiratory metabolism and iron–sulfur protein maturation. He has also explored nickel chelation against multidrug-resistant enteric bacteria in laboratory and animal-model studies.
affiliation: University of Georgia · Athens, USA

Nickel chelation against multidrug-resistant enteric pathogens

name: Eric P. Skaar
bio: Investigates the struggle between hosts and pathogens for essential nutrients. His laboratory studies bacterial metal acquisition, the action of host metal-binding proteins such as calprotectin, and the metabolic adaptations that support infection.
affiliation: Vanderbilt University Medical Center · Nashville, USA

name: Walter J. Chazin
role: Professor of Biochemistry & Chemistry; Chancellor’s Chair in Medicine
bio: Uses structural biology and biophysics to connect protein structure, dynamics and function. His metal-biology work includes the host-defense protein calprotectin and the molecular basis of antimicrobial metal sequestration.
affiliation: Vanderbilt University · Nashville, USA

name: Thomas E. Kehl-Fie
bio: Investigates how host-imposed nutrient starvation changes bacterial infection. His laboratory studies adaptations that allow Staphylococcus aureus to overcome metal restriction, and how nutritional immunity changes susceptibility to host defenses and antibiotics.
affiliation: University of Iowa · Iowa City, USA

name: Michael D. L. Johnson
bio: Investigates how bacteria process, sense and maintain metals during infection. His laboratory connects microbial metal homeostasis with the host environment and potential antibacterial strategies, including the response of Streptococcus pneumoniae to copper.
affiliation: University of Arizona · Tucson, USA

name: Elizabeth M. Nolan
bio: Investigates the chemical competition for metals between hosts and microbes. Her work examines antimicrobial metal sequestration by calprotectin, bacterial siderophores and metallophores, and strategies for using iron-acquisition pathways to deliver antibiotics.
affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology · Cambridge, USA

name: Dianne K. Newman
role: Binder/Amgen Professor of Biology and Geobiology; Merkin Institute Professor
bio: Studies bioenergetics and the cell biology of metabolically diverse bacteria. Her work links electron transfer and redox-active metabolites with microbial communities, including biofilms in chronic infections and crop rhizospheres.
affiliation: California Institute of Technology · Pasadena, USA

name: Kenneth H. Nealson
bio: Studies microbial physiology, environmental microbiology and the genomics of natural populations. His foundational work on metal-reducing bacteria helped establish Shewanella as a model for extracellular electron transfer and microbial fuel cells.
affiliation: University of Southern California · Los Angeles, USA

name: Jeffrey A. Gralnick
bio: Investigates extracellular electron transfer in Shewanella and related microbes. Work on secreted flavins, electron-transfer machinery and bacterial physiology connects basic microbial metabolism with metal reduction and applied biotechnology.
affiliation: University of Minnesota · St. Paul, USA

name: Derek R. Lovley
bio: Studies the physiology and ecology of anaerobic microorganisms. Work on Geobacter and extracellular electron transfer connects metal reduction with groundwater bioremediation, microbial fuel cells and the development of biological electronic materials.
affiliation: University of Massachusetts Amherst · Amherst, USA

name: Gemma Reguera
role: Professor; Associate Dean for Faculty Affairs and Development
bio: Studies how microbes adapt to environmental change and applies that knowledge to bioremediation, bioenergy and nanotechnology. Her group investigates electroactive microbes, microbial communities that remove agrochemicals, and the behavior of human-associated microbiomes.
affiliation: Michigan State University · East Lansing, USA

name: Joseph A. Caruso
role: Distinguished Research Professor; Director, Metallomics Center of the Americas
bio: Advanced elemental speciation and ICP-MS-based metallomics through analytical methods that connect chromatography with mass spectrometry. His work helped make it possible to ask which chemical forms of metals occur in biological samples, rather than measuring total elemental abundance alone.
affiliation: University of Cincinnati · Cincinnati, USA

name: Ryszard Łobiński
bio: Develops analytical approaches for detecting, identifying and quantifying trace-metal species in biological and environmental systems. His work helped establish metallomics and links mass spectrometry, chemical speciation and systems microbiology.
affiliation: CNRS / University of Pau · Pau, France

name: Joanna Szpunar
role: FTMS Bio platform lead, IPREM / UPPA
bio: Develops high-resolution mass-spectrometry approaches for metal, metalloid and biomolecule speciation. The FTMS Bio platform she leads applies Fourier-transform mass spectrometry to environmental and health questions, including molecular identification and quantitative analysis.
affiliation: CNRS / University of Pau · Pau, France

name: Uwe Karst
bio: Develops analytical methods for metal speciation and chemical imaging of biological tissues. His group combines laser-ablation ICP-MS, electrochemistry and mass spectrometry to investigate the distribution and transformation of metals and metal-containing compounds.
affiliation: University of Münster · Münster, Germany

name: Detlef Günther
role: Professor of Trace Element & Micro Analysis
bio: A leading developer of laser-ablation ICP-MS instrumentation and imaging methods that underpin spatially resolved elemental and metallomic analysis.
affiliation: ETH Zurich · Zurich, Switzerland

name: Manuela Raffatellu
bio: Studies the competition between intestinal pathogens and the microbiota. Her research connects Salmonella colonization, inflammation and nutrient acquisition, including the ways host iron- and metal-withholding defenses reshape microbial competition in the gut.
affiliation: University of California San Diego · La Jolla, USA

name: Andreas J. Bäumler
bio: Studies the ecological and metabolic mechanisms that allow enteric pathogens to colonize the intestine. His work connects inflammation, nutrient availability and bacterial competition, helping explain why Salmonella and related organisms can expand when gut conditions change.
affiliation: University of California Davis · Davis, USA

name: Karen Pendergrass
bio: Founder and Standards Architect of ICS, and architect of the Heavy Metal Index evidence system. Her work connects contaminant occurrence, microbial metal biology and standards methodology. She develops the research frameworks and editorial perspective behind this guide; her DOI-registered preprints are identified by their publication status.
affiliation: Heavy Metal Index · Institute of Contaminant Standards (ICS)

name: Kimberly Eyer
affiliation: Institute of Contaminant Standards (ICS)
bio: Co-founder of ICS and a member of its executive leadership, with a public record as a co-author of certification standards. Her Microbiome Medicine profile describes a professional nursing background. She is a co-author on research records featured in this guide.
